New Zealand are showing the Diamonds the way to unlock this Jamaican defence with some deft, speedy passing which has given the Silver Ferns a 16-13 lead at quarter-time in the gold medal game.

The Diamonds struggled mightily to get the ball past Shamera Sterling-Humphrey in their semi-final on Saturday but the Silver Ferns had few issues until Sterling-Humphrey intercepted a pass in the final seconds of the term.

Perhaps, Jamaica will storm back as they are very much good enough to do that but the Silver Ferns have looked the more settled side so far while the passing of Grace Heffernan and Maddy Gordon has allowed Grace Nweke to have plenty of close shots at goal where she has made 14 of 14 shots.

World.title: Putting faith in the paper trail
World.content:
“Not old (C8), just confused,” says Meri Will of Baulkham Hills. “I’ve been informed that my church’s payroll and HR systems will be inaccessible for three weeks while the transfer to a new service provider takes place. Timesheets and leave applications during this time must be submitted via paper forms. Sounds refreshingly simple, except that the only address given is an email one.”

“A colleague told me recently that what made him feel old was his son announcing that he had applied for a Seniors Card,” adds Jim Pollitt of Wahroonga. Ann Clydsdale of Bathurst got it when running into a former student: “They had their grandchildren with them, and said children were well past the toddler stage.”

Helen Lewin of Tumbi Umbi is familiar with copping a different lingo abroad (C8): “Back in 1982 we did a tour of a Schloss overlooking Salzburg. It was done in German but could have been Greek to me. Some weeks later while looking for something to do on a rainy day in Cognac (just drinking was out of the question) we went to the local cinema to rewatch Star Wars. Majorly disappointed to discover Luke and Han had been dubbed into French.” Étoile de la Mort approche!

The naming of the Australian Underwater Hockey team (C8) continues, starting with John Perry of Newtown: “May I suggest The Australian Fur Sealaroos? Shortened to AFSes if the full title is too much of a mouthful?”, while both Roz Millar of Moss Vale and Bart Fielden of Avoca Beach are keen on The Platypuses, with Roz suggesting The Plats for short. Add an extra T, and you’re looking at a potential sponsorship with the added possibility of free board shorts.

We were pondering the suitability of the beloved monotreme when Don Bain of Port Macquarie came along: “As unique to our continent as the kangaroo or the wallaby, is the platypus, and, when I discovered that a platypus can remain underwater for a full half-minute, unaided, it suggested itself as a fitting nickname for the national underwater hockey team. Needless to say, The Platypussies held no appeal, but an indigenous name for our duck-billed amphibian rang true. Let’s hear it for The Boondaburras!”

World.title: Mother sobs alongside 12-year-old son as he’s remanded over alleged assault on good Samaritan
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Mother sobs alongside 12-year-old son as he’s remanded over alleged assault on good Samaritan Nicole Precel and Eleanor Campbell Updated August 2, 2026 — 8:33pm ,first published 4:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Five teenagers have been charged after an assault in Melbourne’s west that left a good Samaritan in a critical condition. Victoria Police said three boys, aged 12, 13 and 15, and two girls, both aged 14, had allegedly tried to steal items from a shop on Hampshire Road in Sunshine just after 2pm on Saturday. A 60-year-old man, who was working nearby, came to the aid of a shop worker, who was in a scuffle in the street over the goods. It’s alleged the man, who remained in a critical condition in the Royal Melbourne Hospital on Sunday night, was set upon by the teens. The teens, from the Brimbank and Banyule area, who cannot be named, have been charged with affray, violent disorder, intentionally causing serious injury and intentionally causing injury.



Four teens were arrested near the incident by protective service officers and members of the transit safety division, while the 12-year-old boy was arrested at his home on Saturday night. On Sunday afternoon, Magistrate Robyn Hamilton adjourned remands for the accused until August 7. “Their young age is a very upsetting factor,” she said. “It’s inevitable that in this case there will be different charges and in that case, you know that I may refuse bail in those circumstances.” The 12-year-old boy and his mother sobbed as the magistrate remanded the young boy. The magistrate noted that “within hours or days the victim will die.”



“This is not children just, you know, engaging in assault and running off,” she said. “This is a case where the victim is left in an unsurvivable situation. It really doesn’t get any more serious than that.” The incident comes just days after Victoria’s new premier, Ben Carroll, pledged a crackdown on anyone who abuses, intimidates or assaults retail, fast-food and transport workers in their workplace. The new laws, which were introduced in July, mean culprits could face a ban from those workplaces for 12 months. Anyone who breaches the bans could face up to two years’ prison or a fine of up to $50,000. On Sunday morning, speaking at the opening of the Ambulatory Care Centre at the Northern Hospital before charges had been laid, Carroll said the teens should face adult time if convicted.



“This was terrible what occurred to this gentleman in a retail shop,” he said. Premier Ben Carroll speaks to the media at the nearly completed new Northern Hospital Ambulatory Care Centre, Epping. Chris Hopkins “That’s why there is no tolerance for this sort of behaviour, it’s awful, and lifetime consequences for them, but also the offenders. It’s going to have lifetime consequences for you, because your life will be changed when you face jail time, and you’ve got to think and make sure you do not do this sort of behaviour. It is simply unacceptable.” Carroll said his first priority as premier was the Big Build royal commission, his second was community safety. He said he was committed to ensuring community safety was “fundamental to everything we do”.



“We are working very hard. I met with the chief commissioner last week, and I’ve told him he’ll have every resource he needs to help us tackle violent crime,” the premier said. World.title: ‘Forever in the mountain’: Melbourne hiker, 28, found dead on US trail
World.content:
NationalTragedy ‘Forever in the mountain’: Melbourne hiker, 28, found dead on US trail Isabel McMillan and Eleanor Campbell August 2, 2026 — 8:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

William Standish lived for hiking. His passion took him all over the world – Sweden, Nepal, Papua New Guinea, Canada and the US, to mention a few. At just 28 years old, the young Melburnian dreamed of moving to South America to live and work. First, though, he wanted to complete a gruelling walk – one that he first attempted but was forced to abandon two years ago. William Standish was found dead on a Wyoming hiking trail last week. It was on this trail – the Continental Divide Trail from Canada to Mexico – that he was reported missing. His family hadn’t heard from him in days, and when a rescue crew went out to look for him, they confirmed the worst. “He felt deeply, loved genuinely and always, always made people feel seen.” Statement from family of Will Standish



“Our beautiful Will was a treasure,” his family told this masthead in a statement on Sunday night. “He was funny, cheeky, adorable, smart and kind. Unapologetically himself.” “He felt deeply, loved genuinely and always, always made people feel seen.” Earlier this year, Standish had embarked on his second attempt at the gruelling hike that begins in Canada, after injuring his foot during the same hike in 2024 and heading home earlier than planned. Now, Standish’s heart and soul will be “forever in the mountain”, his family said in a statement, after a horror fall claimed his life on the trail. According to his family, Will had a strong passion for social justice and was profoundly connected with nature. He studied environmental sciences and once spent a semester abroad in the Czech Republic.



“We want to thank the tireless efforts of the Search and Rescue teams who found him and the authorities who are caring for him until we can bring him home,” they said. “Finally, a note from us to our Will. We love you. We will carry you with us forever. Thank you for filling our lives with a love so deep, so full of colour and warmth. “Rest in eternal sunshine. Dance with the stars.” Will Standish pictured with his father Dave. After 8am US time on Wednesday, Teton County Search and Rescue, based in Jackson, Wyoming, found a body, nearly a week after a 28-year-old Australian hiker had been reported missing on a remote part of the trail between Yellowstone and Grand Teton National Parks.



In a statement, the rescue group said they were saddened to report the man, later identified as Standish, had died after a suspected fall on the trail, in an area known as “the Wigwams, on the west slope of the Tetons”. “Evidence suggests that he may have fallen from a steep, high-altitude ridgeline that separates Grand Teton National Park and the Jedediah Smith Wilderness,” the rescue group’s statement said. Officials from the national parks, who led the investigation, said Standish had been attempting to hike the Continental Divide Trail – a hike starting in Canada through to the border of Mexico. This time, he was hiking southbound, after his initial northbound attempt in 2024. Standish had been giving his family back home in Australia regular updates via his Garmin, with an update sent on July 19 planning out his next movements. On July 23, his family received a check-in with no coordinates or message, but a video on Facebook Messenger, which they believed placed him in the Tetons. By July 27, when they hadn’t heard anything else, they contacted park officials.



By Wednesday morning, two days later, the search and rescue helicopter flew a team to Standish’s last presumed point, and, from the air, saw a bright orange backpack. Then, they found him. “His body was recovered and transported to TCSAR headquarters in Jackson before being transferred to the Teton County Coroner’s Office,” the rescue group said. Will (left) with his siblings Jess and George. “TCSAR sends its sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased, and wishes to express its gratitude to the partnering federal agencies who assisted in the investigation.” Sharing her grief, trail friend Katie Jackson also took to social media to farewell the hiker, who she said had a “uniquely large heart”.



“Struck this week by the enormity of the choices we make: where we go, what we do, and especially who we go with,” she wrote. “Incredibly grateful to have known Will so well and experienced how his life touched and changed mine. “Will had a uniquely large heart that was filled to the brim with love from and for his family, friends, adventures, tiny foster puppies, music, snowboarding, and comically large burritos. To know him was to spend most of your day laughing.” Will Standish pictured with his mum Ann. The Continental Divide Trail Coalition said they’d lost someone who lifted everyone up.



“The CDT community lost a bit of light this week,” they said in a Facebook post following his death. “Though he began his 2026 hike stronger than ever, Will was reported overdue on July 26. Concerned hikers immediately rallied to spread the word and join the search, which was a bit of comfort to his worried family in Australia. “At CDTC, like so many others, we are deeply saddened by the news of Will’s passing.” Since his death in the US, Standish’s trail friends started a fundraiser to help pay for his funeral, and the heavy price of bringing him home to Australia. Will Standish (middle) pictured with siblings Jess and George, his dad Dave, and his mum Ann.



A DFAT spokesperson said they were providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian who died in Wyoming. “We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time,” they said in a statement. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Holes in medical safety net: Millions of machines, thousands of problems, a few dozen staff
World.content:
An investigation into medical devices reveals alarming flaws in both the machines we put in our bodies and the system that oversees them. See all stories .

The watchdog overseeing the safety and efficacy of hundreds of thousands of medical devices has drastically fewer staff than it predicted it would need to cope with an expected surge in reports of problems in hospitals. An investigation into the Therapeutic Goods Administration, which monitors adverse event reports from 1.4 million medical devices in use around Australia, shows the federal government refused to approve additional funding to cope with the increase in reports despite concerns the regulator was already understaffed. Clockwise from top left: Malfunctioning medical devices that have led to patient injuries include the Dexcom G7 glucose-monitoring device, SynchroMed II intrathecal pain pump, Euky Bear humidifier and CellAED defibrillator. Mark Stehle A document obtained under Freedom of Information shows that in 2024, the TGA’s team monitoring the tens of thousands of “adverse event” alerts it receives every year was missing half its budgeted staff and was struggling to fill the roles. On top of that, the 2024 document warns the TGA had expected up to a tenfold increase in alerts when a mandatory reporting regime for hospitals started in March this year.



Managing the seven most time-consuming steps of dealing with those reports could take up to 150 extra staff members, the internal documents estimate. Without improvements to the agency’s IT systems, the extra cost to screen the reports could run up to $15.8 million a year. At the time the document was written, the team in charge of the reports was “operating about 50 per cent allocated FTE [full-time staff equivalents], indicating that recruitment alone could be a significant challenge to the organisation”. Part of the reason for the staffing burden was explained in another document – a presentation from 2025 – exposing significant issues with the TGA’s information technology and data-handling systems.



The revelations about the TGA’s resourcing issues come as this masthead’s Medical Malfuctions investigation has revealed major loopholes in Australia’s approvals system that allows devices with little to no clinical evidence to be sold to patients. Once approved for sale, medical devices with flaws are meant to be caught by the TGA’s “post-market” system, which monitors reports of side effects to spot problematic devices. The documents released under freedom of information show this safety net, which gathers so-called “adverse events”, is strained. The 2025 TGA presentation on the regulator’s adverse event surveillance team found “missing information and underreporting lead to difficulties with using adverse event data, and limit its reliability”.



“The use of adverse event data to answer questions and inform teams’ work is limited due to its accessibility, usability and presentation,” it says. And crucially, “systems lack the functionality to alert teams of trends and risk factors to inform targeted work”. The documents also detail issues with IT systems including the use of several different legacy databases to process reports, each report requiring a large number of steps to input; and that systems do not talk to each other. They also report staff saying the system goes down once a week; processing a single report takes at least 85 minutes; and the software lacks the ability to alert investigators to trends in injuries or deaths.



Of 37,540 adverse event reports received between 2019 and 2023, the TGA investigated just 4.2 per cent. “The TGA usually does not do much investigation at all. They include it in the database. It is logged just in case it becomes very frequent,” said a person with direct knowledge of the process, speaking anonymously to avoid reprisal. Loading This masthead’s Medical Malfunctions investigation used artificial intelligence to scrape thousands of these adverse event reports to detail issues with a number of devices including a portable defibrillator, glucose monitors and spinal pain pumps. The investigation also discovered the TGA’s public Database of Adverse Event Notifications was missing dozens of deaths reported before October 2019, forcing the regulator to publish a warning about a “technical issue” with the database.



In response to questions, the TGA confirmed it had made a budget request for additional funding to handle the influx from hospital reports. That was rejected by the government, but the agency said it did now have 30 staff members in its monitoring team. Tracey Duffy, first assistant secretary of the TGA’s medical devices and product quality division, said the reports did not reflect the agency’s current conditions. Duffy said the TGA had significantly increased staff levels since the 2024 report was authored but conceded some of its systems required investment. “At the TGA, we’re dealing with quite a few old IT systems. We’re in a journey of transformation and modernisation when it comes to our IT systems,” she told this masthead.



“They are limited in the sense of being able to do things in the most effective way. It takes more time, more resources, more training. It is taking additional staff to be able to do those processes.” That’s left the agency reliant on funding from the Department of Health to install a temporary software solution. “We have sufficient funding that allows us to put in place a workable system,” said Duffy. She said the level of investigation of adverse events was “appropriate given the risk we have in place”.



Health Minister Mark Butler said the TGA was allocated departmental funding for its adverse event system to cope with the increased load from hospital reporting. It comes as this masthead’s investigation into medical devices has triggered calls for the establishment of clinical registries for pain devices – to prove if they truly are safe and effective. Last month, this masthead reported on Medtronic’s SynchroMed II pain pump, which remains registered for sale despite a lack of high-quality data showing it is effective at treating pain. The pump is associated with significant complication rates, including a rare risk of paralysis. That prompted calls from both the Australian Pain Society and the Faculty of Pain Medicine for the establishment of registries for pain devices like the SynchroMed II, to allowing outcomes to be tracked over time, including how well they work and side effects.



Related Investigation

Medical Malfunctions Medical Malfunctions “The Australian Pain Society supports a national registry for implantable pain devices,” Pain Society president Bernadette Smith said. “Reliable, transparent data on safety, effectiveness and patient outcomes is essential to inform decision-making and ensure people living with pain receive care guided by the best available evidence.” The only existing pain register, known as EPPOC, tracks outcomes for patients at the nation’s specialist pain services. It faces closure after funding from the NSW state government expired. “It would seem to reflect a lack of interest from funding bodies in whether or not pain treatments actually work,” said Dr Chris Hayes, director of the Hunter Integrated Pain Service in Newcastle, and former dean of Australia’s Faculty of Pain Medicine. World.title: Fraser ‘disrupted’ the process. But could he achieve what only one other man has this century?
World.content:
Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 Fraser ‘disrupted’ the process. But could he achieve what only one other man has this century? Peter Ryan August 2, 2026 — 7:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Josh Fraser was expected to lay strong foundations for Michael Voss’s replacement. Nothing is as simple as that.

The message to be patient with North Melbourne is wearing thin.

What Nick Watson could achieve that Peter Daicos didn’t.

Essendon are about as deserving of an assistance package as a billionaire seeking tax relief.

Tasmania went for the mature-aged recruit when they appointed Ken Hinkley as their first coach. Essendon’s coach recruiters are conducting their coaching search in the equivalent of a compromised draft. That’s because several strong candidates declared themselves off-limits to the Bombers due to both the campaign supporting James Hird as a candidate and the club’s perceived treatment of “outsiders”. Josh Fraser’s record as Blues interim coach is outstanding. AFL Photos



By contrast Carlton appeared to have a free run to appoint the best untried coach in the market via a process being managed by experienced operators – chief executive Graham Wright and football boss Chris Davies. A predictable process loomed. Coffee dates at Brunetti’s and elsewhere, followed by a short list of candidates presenting in the next fortnight would lead to a new polo top being measured up and worn by a new coach declaring at a media conference their excitement at what lay ahead. Meanwhile, Josh Fraser was expected to selflessly take on the interim job for 14 matches and lay strong foundations for Michael Voss’s replacement. Of course, nothing is that simple nowadays.



Fraser has the Blues inside the top 10 with three games remaining after their 76-point thrashing of the Brisbane Lions became their ninth win in 11 matches under the hoodie-wearing coach. Reflecting the times, he has disrupted – by winning rather than campaigning – a coaching selection process that you could argue he should have been considered for before his wins as interim coach. Or has he? Those who joined the ‘give it to him now’ category after the Blues’ massive win over Brisbane think Fraser has done the unthinkable and made the Essendon coaching race more open than Carlton’s. That’s a stretch.



What Fraser has done is earn himself an invitation to join the short list of candidates to become Carlton’s next coach. He might even earn himself the right to be in the last two considered. It would be a surprise if he didn’t accept that invitation this week after consulting family, friends, mentors and the Blues as he has done throughout his time in the chair. Assistant coach Jaymie Graham is a candidate for both the Carlton and Essendon coaching jobs. AFL Photos Fraser deserves that chance to present, but he also should be respected if he decides the time is not right for him. He has been in the coaching business since 2013, coached his own teams at NEAFL and VFL level and has an ability to create genuine relationships with people across all levels of the game.



His authenticity, perspective and humility has shone through during his more regular public appearances as interim coach and, unlike some other interim coaches in recent times, he has wanted to divert attention away from himself at every opportunity. That’s been good to see as Fraser put his coaching reputation on the line when he did the right thing by the Blues in accepting the interim position for 14 matches. His ability as a coach was going to be judged despite his capacity to create the environment he believed necessary for success being limited. But he took it on anyway. Fraser is not silly. He knows enough about coaching and the AFL to understand that nine wins from 11 matches doesn’t automatically make him the best man for the job. The 44-year-old would be as aware as the hard heads responsible for selecting Carlton’s next coach (which also includes Eagles’ premiership coach Adam Simpson) that the wins/loss record as interim is just one part of the criteria assessed when deciding the best candidate.



Carlton CEO Graham Wright, president Rob Priestley and football manager Chris Davies have a big decision ahead of them. Getty Images The panel wants to know what the candidates stand for as a coach, their use of data and how it informs their decision-making, their management skills, their capacity to cope with pressure, their ability to teach in a range of ways and a range of other qualities that make senior coaches successful. Carlton have been able to see the way Fraser operates as the stand-in coach but will still be making as educated a guess about him in a range of those areas as they will be on the other known candidates which include James Kelly, Corey Enright, Daniel Giansiracusa and Jaymie Graham. Like Fraser, that crew will have strengths and weaknesses and will need the support of experienced leaders if they become a senior coach. Unlike Fraser they won’t have proved themselves as able to coach a winning team at AFL level and their ability to form relationships with the players will be unknown.



To many supporters that will be all that matters and, in many ways, it is all that is important. Choosing an untried coach other than Fraser will be a harder sell and need explanation, but they will be able to do that if they select another person after comparing the candidate’s methods and personality. If they choose Fraser they need to know he impressed them enough to convince them he was the best candidate. A coach who can lead this team to a premiership is what Carlton are chasing. Of the nine interim coaches appointed full-time this century, Paul Roos is the only interim coach to do so. Fraser may, in fact, be the man.



The reality is the next fortnight will help inform Carlton’s decision as much if not more than the past 11 matches. Whatever the Blues’ call, the past three months has convinced everyone that at some point, somewhere, Fraser, if he wishes to, should become a senior coach. And it should also remind Essendon of the job talented coaches working away in the system can do if given the chance. North Melbourne are treading water, regardless of what they say In the past five matches, North Melbourne have been sixth in the competition for average age and fifth for games experience.



They have been competitive but lost each game. Although there is a big hole in the middle when it comes to age and experience, they should be performing better than they have in the past five matches when a wildcard chance has been up for grabs. Their inaccuracy has been costly but combined with the overuse of handball and indefensible turnovers in the back half, they have collapsed to 13th on the ladder. Billboards promoting improvement aren’t created from two wins over Essendon and Richmond, Carlton on Good Friday, Port Adelaide, Gold Coast and West Coast. Alastair Clarkson faces his moment of truth this off season at the Kangaroos. AFL Photos



Making mistakes is part of learning but some of the risky kicks their defensive runners take from the back half would be off the table even for defenders at the best, most skilful and experienced teams. It works often enough for their transition numbers to be reasonable but too often mistakes are made at crucial moments when the result is in doubt. It’s not just Colby McKercher and Caleb Daniel biting off more than they can chew, but that pair need to be accountable so the team learns when to go and when to slow. After 19 wins in 79 matches as North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson looks exasperated on game day, his unrelenting style potentially wearing on his leaders who play with furrowed brows in 2026. He reached that point at the Hawks in his first two seasons before switching gear.



Perhaps that’s the conversation the club hierarchy needs to have with him before entering next season. They can’t extend him prematurely but the four-time premiership coach who joined them in their hour of need deserves honesty as to what they are thinking. And if they are considering that a new breed of coach could do for North Melbourne what Steven King has done for Melbourne this season then that argument must be had. The Kangaroos need to be honest with each other over summer so the alignment necessary for success is maintained. Because the message to be patient is wearing thin.



Don’t sell Nick Watson’s achievement short Nick Watson is a star. He can turn a match in a minute, his ability to switch from defensive to attacking transition is unmatched. He is brave, cheeky and skilful. His effort to kick 52 goals with three rounds remaining is meritorious because few small forwards reach the half century before turning 22. Nick Watson was at his brilliant best yet again for the Hawks. Getty Images Brisbane Lions champion Luke Power kicked 52 goals before turning 21 in 2000, but he is the only one this century to do so at a younger age than Watson.



Cyril Rioli never kicked 50 goals in a season, Luke Breust was aged 23 when he passed the milestone. Eddie Betts was even older than Breust. Jeff Farmer and Phil Matera were 23 and Stephen Milne had turned 22. Ty Stengle helped the Cats to a flag with 50 goals in 2022 aged 23. Peter Daicos, a mid-sized forward, had kicked 70 goals before he turned 20 in 1981. Daicos was a goalkicking freak. If Watson can win the Coleman Medal, he will have done something Daicos didn’t. Pick one is enough of a helping hand for the Bombers



Essendon have draft pick number one with three matches remaining after the Tigers’ win over an inaccurate West Coast. Finishing on the bottom will help the AFL justify an assistance package despite the Bombers being about as deserving of one as a billionaire seeking tax relief. Essendon have high hopes for Nate Caddy AFL Photos Giving them assistance is not only a reward for mediocrity but investing in a club that, part from recent recruiting, is yet to prove they can stack good decision after good decision as yet. Before any assistance package, the Bombers will have pick one, a likely compensation pick early in the second round which is designed to help clubs rebuilding plus any return from trading Zach Merrett who appears set to exit.



That will arrive just one season after they added Sullivan Robey, Jacob Farrow and Dyson Sharp with picks 9, 10 and 13, following Isaac Kako in 2024 and Nate Caddy in 2023. Injuries have affected their performance and they missed on a couple of high draft picks. Fair play to Essendon for asking, but there should be resistance to assistance inside AFL House. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Bomber suffers concussion in friendly fire clash; Dees grind out win on Gold Coast; Tigers off the bottom
World.content:
AFL Briefing SportAFLAFL 2026 Bomber suffers concussion in friendly fire clash; Dees grind out win on Gold Coast; Tigers off the bottom Daniel Brettig, Peter Ryan, Ed Jackson Marc McGowan and Updated August 2, 2026 — 10:35pm ,first published 2:46pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Adelaide surged into the top four for the first time this year by dishing out a 72-point belting of an outclassed Essendon.

A West Coast player went to ground in obvious pain after a gut punch from a Richmond opponent at the MCG.

Surgery for Swan after suffering a sickening lower leg injury. Young Bomber Angus Clarke was taken to hospital after suffering a concussion and neck injury in a collision with a teammate as Adelaide surged into the top four for the first time this year by dishing out a 72-point belting of Essendon at Marvel Stadium. Following a disquieting home defeat to Collingwood last week, the Crows were all business against the struggling Bombers, absorbing a first quarter challenge before growing their margin at every change to move ahead of Brisbane and Melbourne on percentage. Essendon’s Angus Clarke reels after getting a knock. AFL Photos Clarke, 19, has faced a spate of injuries this year and seemed to have shrugged off one when he hyperextended a knee early on. But he then clashed inadvertently with Isaac Kako, resulting in a concussion and an apparent neck problem that interim coach Dean Solomon said was serious enough to send him to hospital.



“His year’s been really interrupted with injury, the foot initially, gets back in the side for two or three, gets a head knock,” Solomon said. “There is concussion there but also a bit of soreness in the neck. “So they’re going to take him to hospital now to check further and make sure there’s no real damage there. It’s frustrating for him because he’s a really good young man and he’s hungry to be a good player ... he just can’t get continuity in his game.” Adelaide’s senior assistant coach Murray Davis is a contender to take over as Essendon coach, and he did his chances no harm by ensuring that Solomon would oversee another heavy defeat. Crows coach Matthew Nicks said Davis would be welcome to stay at the Crows for the remainder of the year even if he was chosen for the Essendon job ahead of candidates including James Hird. Adelaide’s Izak Rankine. Getty Images “I think that’s up to Murray, and the reason it’s up to Murray is I trust him completely,” Nicks said.



“If he wants to be with us we’d love him to stay with us and work right through. He deserves that. He’s been incredible for what he’s done for us the last couple [of] seasons. So we’d love him to stay on, but we also wish him all the best if that is the opportunity that shows up.” The Crows may also have unearthed a useful role player for the pointy end of the season, with 21-year-old debutant Oscar Ryan finding plenty of the ball and kicking a memorable first goal in the third term. Skipper Jordan Dawson shrugged off an attempted tag by Mason Redman to be the prime midfield mover for the Crows, who were sweating on the seriousness of yet another hamstring complaint - this time for young defender James Borlase. Riley Thilthorpe kicked five goals for Adelaide, while Callum Ah Chee was a lively presence up forward in only his fifth appearance of the year after joining the Crows from Brisbane. Two-metre Peter Wright presented a strong marking target for Essendon with six majors, while Zach Merrett also worked hard. Kako may find himself under the spotlight of the match review panel after a tackle that dumped Adelaide defender Josh Worrell’s head into the Docklands turf.



Before the game, Crows senior coach Matthew Nicks had conceded there was some merit in how former Pies coach Mick Malthouse had critiqued his team’s poor display against Collingwood as “horribly soft”. “Mick’s comments were warranted, I could feel what Micky Malthouse was talking about, he’s a very experienced head, he knows what he sees in footy,” Nicks told Fox Footy. “We rate ourselves highly in that toughness area but we did drop away in that second half, so what he said was warranted. Little was proven either way against the Bombers, but the improved ladder position will help. “We look at results yesterday and we don’t shy away from the fact that opportunity is now there,” Nicks said post-match. “If you win all three games then it’s ours. That’s easier said than done. “We’ve just got to continue to win now, our destiny is in our hands. In a way we’ve earned the position we’re in, we’ve now got three weeks to nail that, starting next weekend.”



Demons grind out win on Gold Coast Ed Jackson Melbourne have survived a major scare to defeat Gold Coast by nine points at People First Stadium and keep their AFL top four hopes on track. In a see-sawing match with multiple lead changes, the Demons did just enough in the fourth quarter to claim an 18.6 (114) to 16.9 (105) win on Sunday. Jacob van Rooyen and Harrison Petty each kicked three goals for the visitors, who were clinical with their shots on goal throughout.



Max Gawn was dominant for the Demons with 25 disposals, 10 marks, 33 hitouts and nine clearances while Trent Rivers and Jake Bowey led the disposals for the Demons with 29 touches apiece. Kysaiah Pickett of the Demons shows plenty of dash, finding space ahead of Matt Rowell. Getty Images Jed Walter kicked three for the Suns, all in the first half, as Gold Coast were unable to prevent slumping to their 10th straight defeat in what was Christian Petracca’s first match against his former club. Petracca, whose impact on the Suns was under the spotlight throughout the week following an on-field argument with young gun Leo Lombard in the defeat to Carlton, had minimal impact on the contest with 16 disposals and two clearances. Instead it was John Noble (34 disposals, seven tackles, 10 marks) and Matt Rowell (30 disposals, nine tackles, eight clearances) who led the way for the Suns, who fought hard but couldn’t hold off the fast-finishing Demons to end their losing run.



Melbourne set the template for their accuracy in front of goal early, kicking five straight in the opening term to hold a three-point lead at the first break. View post on X Bailey Humphrey’s goal after the siren at the end of the second quarter, despite a question mark over whether he ran off the line of the mark as he came into kick, had the hosts in front heading into the main break. And the Suns extended that lead to three goals during a high-scoring third term, kicking four goals alone from free kicks. The Demons, however, kicked two goals in the last 30 seconds including another after-the-siren major to Petty to snatch a one-point lead heading into the final quarter.



A nasty looking fall early in the fourth quarter forced Blake Howes from the field clutching his left wrist but it didn’t deter the Demons, who kicked four goals to three to secure the points. Suns defender Sam Collins (ribs) failed to return after sustaining a hit to his side in a marking contest with Ed Langdon in the second quarter. AAP Tiger in the gun for behind-the-play blow Marc McGowan



Richmond took a major step towards dodging a second wooden spoon in three years with a second win this season over a wayward West Coast as Tigers defender Luke Trainor faces match review scrutiny for a gut punch. Adem Yze’s men had lost eight matches in a row by an average of almost 50 points, and were on the bottom, behind Essendon on percentage, with a miserable 2-17 win-loss record before Sunday’s 11-point victory. Richmond took advantage of the Eagles’ yips in front of goal at the MCG to climb above the Bombers and within one win of 16th-placed West Coast, who had kicked 3.17 at one stage before losing 12.12 (84) to 9.19 (73). The result eases pressure on coach Yze, who has presided over only 10 victories in 66 matches in what is a full-blown rebuild at Tigerland.



“We’re rebuilding, so when you rebuild, you need games into younger players,” Yze said. “We get a win today, but we still need Jonty Faull, Harry Armstrong and Tom Sims [to get back from injury] … we’ve still got guys we need to gel together. But at the same time, if we can scratch out some wins while we’re going through what we’re going through with unavailability – it’s terrific. “We know what we’ve got within our four walls … we’ve dealt with more than what other teams have dealt with. “But when you see Sammy [Lalor] do what he does today; he’s [only] scratching the surface. When those lads start to grow together; it’ll be really exciting.” Footy with feeling: Richmond’s Sam Lalor after kicking the sealer. Getty Images



Yze re-signed until the end of 2028 in November last year, and chief executive Shane Dunne said last month he had the club’s backing. There were only 12 points between the sides at three-quarter-time, but goals to Richmond premiership veterans Tom Lynch (20 disposals, 2.4) and Toby Nankervis blew the margin out before they withstood a late fightback. The Eagles, who have been competitive most weeks despite their lack of success, have plenty to rue, with Jake Waterman’s 2.6 day – on top of putting another kick out on the full – headlining their woeful goalkicking. Elliot Yeo had a chance to slice the difference to six points with a set shot inside the last two minutes, but sprayed it to the left, only for No.1 draft pick Lalor to seal the contest with his third major after winning a test of strength. View post on X



West Coast were trying to beat Richmond at the MCG for the first time since 2015, but the 33,737 crowd instead were able to celebrate a rare Tigers triumph this season. Tim Taranto led Richmond’s charge with 32 disposals and a game-high 11 clearances, while Harley Reid was outstanding in a losing cause with 34 touches, 20 contested possessions and nine clearances. Mid-season draftee Marcus Herbert (34 disposals) was also prolific for the Eagles. Yze said he had not seen Trainor’s behind-the-play gut punch to West Coast’s Jack Williams in the second quarter. They were engaged in a standing wrestle before Trainor struck the Eagle with a clenched left fist. The second-year Tiger, playing his 30th career game, instantly jogged away while Williams went to ground in obvious pain and went to the bench soon after. Richmond captain Toby Nankervis and Nathan Broad celebrated a rare win in 2026. Getty Images



“I’m not too sure how hard the impact was, but if he’s gone and done something wrong, we’ll look at it,” Yze said. “I think there have been a few fines over the last few occasions when things like this have happened, so hopefully, we can get that type of result. “We don’t want to be losing players through stupidity [when we have so many injuries], so hopefully, it wasn’t too bad. We’ve educated our players, and they understand what’s right and wrong.” It is the type of incident the AFL aimed to stamp out when it announced tribunal changes in February, revealing that incidents where a player strikes another in the chest or stomach were more likely to be graded medium impact and result in suspension. Match review officer Michael Christian has typically graded these incidents as low impact, which led to fines rather than bans.



Richmond’s lengthy injury list includes key defensive options Noah Balta, Josh Gibcus and Campbell Gray, while prized draftee Sam Cumming (ankle) was the latest addition on Sunday. Surgery for ‘devastated’ Swan after leg injury Peter Ryan Sydney Swans defender Will Edwards had surgery on Sunday after suffering a sickening lower leg injury against the Saints on Saturday. Will Edwards was taken from the ground with a broken leg. AFL Photos



Edwards appeared to dislocate his ankle and was carted from the field having received pain medication during the Swans’ 19-point win at Marvel Stadium. Coach Dean Cox described the injury as “devastating” for the 23-year-old, who made his debut this season following a series of leg fractures and infections. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 If the Crows fade away yet again, could this Essendon contender step up? The club is expected to provide more information about the injury and his prognosis after the operation. Midfielder James Rowbottom will also have surgery to repair a broken hand sustained during the match against St Kilda. For the Saints, Jack Silvagni (dislocated shoulder) and Tom De Koning (hip pointer) are in doubt for next Sunday night’s match against their former team, Carlton.

World.title: Motorists opt to avoid the fuel spike by buying an EV
World.content:
Motorists avoiding high-priced petrol are upending the nation’s car market, with half of all new vehicles sold over the past three months either EVs or hybrids. The end of the federal government’s fuel excise cut is expected to push the average cost of unleaded well above $2 a litre at most service stations this week, and the consumer watchdog will monitor prices to guard against unreasonable increases. Sales of EVs and hybrids have matched those of unleaded and diesel-powered vehicles over the past three months. Bloomberg But new figures from the Australian Automobile Association show a history-making turnaround in buyers’ habits. Of the 330,000 new cars bought in the June quarter, 167,840 were traditional internal combustion models and the rest were electric vehicles or hybrids. A year ago, 72 per cent of all new vehicles ran on unleaded or diesel. Battery EVs accounted for just 9.3 per cent of new purchases, while hybrids comprised another 14.9 per cent.



In the June quarter, a fifth of all vehicles bought were battery EVs, 17.6 per cent were hybrids and 10.6 per cent plug-in hybrids. Between the March and June quarters, sales of battery cars more than doubled, from 34,434 to 69,414. Petrol prices through that period actually fell, from a peak of $2.53 a litre to less than $1.60. Related Article Analysis

Electric vehicles EVs reach major milestone – meaning climate goals might not be a bridge too far In the extremely competitive medium SUV market, long dominated by petrol vehicles, EVs and hybrids accounted for almost 80 per cent of all sales through the June quarter. At the beginning of the year, they held 60 per cent of the market. It’s not just new EVs winning over motorists. Prices for second-hand electrics have either remained steady or climbed, while they have dropped for internal combustion vehicles.



The surge in EVs has been driven by the jump in oil prices caused by the US-led war against Iran. Brent crude finished trading last week at almost $US90 a barrel on fresh fears of an increase in attacks on Iran by US forces. Despite the ongoing volatility in oil prices, the federal government’s reduction in fuel excise and heavy vehicle road user charge ended at the weekend. The move will add up to 17¢ a litre to the price of unleaded, taking it well above $2 a litre in most markets. Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the cut in excise, which started in April, had taken the “sting” out of petrol prices when they reached their peak. He said the government was now giving people cost-of-living relief through other measures such as last month’s modest reduction in income tax and extra paid parental leave. Chalmers also warned service stations that the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission would increase surveillance of the sector, watching for any unwarranted sharp increases in petrol prices.



“The regulator will step up its monitoring of fuel price movements,” he said. “Any price increase that can’t be explained will face serious scrutiny from the ACCC. Related Article Electric vehicles Soaring EV sales to shield Australia from fuel shortages “We’ve jacked up the penalties for petrol stations that rip off Australians. They face multimillion-dollar fines if they break the law.” On Sunday, deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume would not be drawn on whether ending the fuel excise discount was correct, arguing instead the government had failed to reduce other inflationary pressures across the economy. “It’s a decision for the government,” she told the ABC. “But Australians are going to feel the pain, there’s no doubt about that.



“They didn’t need to feel this pain because it would have been lessened if we had a more resilient economy and the government had done its fair share of the heavy lifting to get inflation down.” Motorists without an EV can save money by switching to lower-priced fuel. Fresh analysis of the Sydney fuel market by the National Roads and Motorists Association found the gap between the lowest priced unleaded petrol, E10, and premium 98, had reached a record of 29¢ a litre, as retailers extended their margins for the top-priced fuel. The saving on a 55-litre tank compared with premium 98 is about $16. Premium 98 fuel is designed primarily for high-performance or high-compression engines. E10 includes 10 per cent ethanol.



NRMA spokesman Peter Khoury said: “With the excise going up today and the war continuing, finding smart ways to save at the bowser remain critical for many Australians struggling with cost of living pressures. Not paying premium prices for premium fuels if you don’t have to is a great place to start.” Many vehicles that run on petrol that were made after the year 2000 can take E10. However, not all are compatible with the fuel, and motorists should check before filling up. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Putting faith in the paper trail
World.content:
“Not old (C8), just confused,” says Meri Will of Baulkham Hills. “I’ve been informed that my church’s payroll and HR systems will be inaccessible for three weeks while the transfer to a new service provider takes place. Timesheets and leave applications during this time must be submitted via paper forms. Sounds refreshingly simple, except that the only address given is an email one.”

“A colleague told me recently that what made him feel old was his son announcing that he had applied for a Seniors Card,” adds Jim Pollitt of Wahroonga. Ann Clydsdale of Bathurst got it when running into a former student: “They had their grandchildren with them, and said children were well past the toddler stage.”

Helen Lewin of Tumbi Umbi is familiar with copping a different lingo abroad (C8): “Back in 1982 we did a tour of a Schloss overlooking Salzburg. It was done in German but could have been Greek to me. Some weeks later while looking for something to do on a rainy day in Cognac (just drinking was out of the question) we went to the local cinema to rewatch Star Wars. Majorly disappointed to discover Luke and Han had been dubbed into French.” Étoile de la Mort approche!

The naming of the Australian Underwater Hockey team (C8) continues, starting with John Perry of Newtown: “May I suggest The Australian Fur Sealaroos? Shortened to AFSes if the full title is too much of a mouthful?”, while both Roz Millar of Moss Vale and Bart Fielden of Avoca Beach are keen on The Platypuses, with Roz suggesting The Plats for short. Add an extra T, and you’re looking at a potential sponsorship with the added possibility of free board shorts.

We were pondering the suitability of the beloved monotreme when Don Bain of Port Macquarie came along: “As unique to our continent as the kangaroo or the wallaby, is the platypus, and, when I discovered that a platypus can remain underwater for a full half-minute, unaided, it suggested itself as a fitting nickname for the national underwater hockey team. Needless to say, The Platypussies held no appeal, but an indigenous name for our duck-billed amphibian rang true. Let’s hear it for The Boondaburras!”

World.title: Mother sobs alongside 12-year-old son as he’s remanded over alleged assault on good Samaritan
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Mother sobs alongside 12-year-old son as he’s remanded over alleged assault on good Samaritan Nicole Precel and Eleanor Campbell Updated August 2, 2026 — 8:33pm ,first published 4:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Five teenagers have been charged after an assault in Melbourne’s west that left a good Samaritan in a critical condition. Victoria Police said three boys, aged 12, 13 and 15, and two girls, both aged 14, had allegedly tried to steal items from a shop on Hampshire Road in Sunshine just after 2pm on Saturday. A 60-year-old man, who was working nearby, came to the aid of a shop worker, who was in a scuffle in the street over the goods. It’s alleged the man, who remained in a critical condition in the Royal Melbourne Hospital on Sunday night, was set upon by the teens. The teens, from the Brimbank and Banyule area, who cannot be named, have been charged with affray, violent disorder, intentionally causing serious injury and intentionally causing injury.



Four teens were arrested near the incident by protective service officers and members of the transit safety division, while the 12-year-old boy was arrested at his home on Saturday night. On Sunday afternoon, Magistrate Robyn Hamilton adjourned remands for the accused until August 7. “Their young age is a very upsetting factor,” she said. “It’s inevitable that in this case there will be different charges and in that case, you know that I may refuse bail in those circumstances.” The 12-year-old boy and his mother sobbed as the magistrate remanded the young boy. The magistrate noted that “within hours or days the victim will die.”



“This is not children just, you know, engaging in assault and running off,” she said. “This is a case where the victim is left in an unsurvivable situation. It really doesn’t get any more serious than that.” The incident comes just days after Victoria’s new premier, Ben Carroll, pledged a crackdown on anyone who abuses, intimidates or assaults retail, fast-food and transport workers in their workplace. The new laws, which were introduced in July, mean culprits could face a ban from those workplaces for 12 months. Anyone who breaches the bans could face up to two years’ prison or a fine of up to $50,000. On Sunday morning, speaking at the opening of the Ambulatory Care Centre at the Northern Hospital before charges had been laid, Carroll said the teens should face adult time if convicted.



“This was terrible what occurred to this gentleman in a retail shop,” he said. Premier Ben Carroll speaks to the media at the nearly completed new Northern Hospital Ambulatory Care Centre, Epping. Chris Hopkins “That’s why there is no tolerance for this sort of behaviour, it’s awful, and lifetime consequences for them, but also the offenders. It’s going to have lifetime consequences for you, because your life will be changed when you face jail time, and you’ve got to think and make sure you do not do this sort of behaviour. It is simply unacceptable.” Carroll said his first priority as premier was the Big Build royal commission, his second was community safety. He said he was committed to ensuring community safety was “fundamental to everything we do”.



“We are working very hard. I met with the chief commissioner last week, and I’ve told him he’ll have every resource he needs to help us tackle violent crime,” the premier said. World.title: ‘Forever in the mountain’: Melbourne hiker, 28, found dead on US trail
World.content:
NationalTragedy ‘Forever in the mountain’: Melbourne hiker, 28, found dead on US trail Isabel McMillan and Eleanor Campbell August 2, 2026 — 8:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

William Standish lived for hiking. His passion took him all over the world – Sweden, Nepal, Papua New Guinea, Canada and the US, to mention a few. At just 28 years old, the young Melburnian dreamed of moving to South America to live and work. First, though, he wanted to complete a gruelling walk – one that he first attempted but was forced to abandon two years ago. William Standish was found dead on a Wyoming hiking trail last week. It was on this trail – the Continental Divide Trail from Canada to Mexico – that he was reported missing. His family hadn’t heard from him in days, and when a rescue crew went out to look for him, they confirmed the worst. “He felt deeply, loved genuinely and always, always made people feel seen.” Statement from family of Will Standish



“Our beautiful Will was a treasure,” his family told this masthead in a statement on Sunday night. “He was funny, cheeky, adorable, smart and kind. Unapologetically himself.” “He felt deeply, loved genuinely and always, always made people feel seen.” Earlier this year, Standish had embarked on his second attempt at the gruelling hike that begins in Canada, after injuring his foot during the same hike in 2024 and heading home earlier than planned. Now, Standish’s heart and soul will be “forever in the mountain”, his family said in a statement, after a horror fall claimed his life on the trail. According to his family, Will had a strong passion for social justice and was profoundly connected with nature. He studied environmental sciences and once spent a semester abroad in the Czech Republic.



“We want to thank the tireless efforts of the Search and Rescue teams who found him and the authorities who are caring for him until we can bring him home,” they said. “Finally, a note from us to our Will. We love you. We will carry you with us forever. Thank you for filling our lives with a love so deep, so full of colour and warmth. “Rest in eternal sunshine. Dance with the stars.” Will Standish pictured with his father Dave. After 8am US time on Wednesday, Teton County Search and Rescue, based in Jackson, Wyoming, found a body, nearly a week after a 28-year-old Australian hiker had been reported missing on a remote part of the trail between Yellowstone and Grand Teton National Parks.



In a statement, the rescue group said they were saddened to report the man, later identified as Standish, had died after a suspected fall on the trail, in an area known as “the Wigwams, on the west slope of the Tetons”. “Evidence suggests that he may have fallen from a steep, high-altitude ridgeline that separates Grand Teton National Park and the Jedediah Smith Wilderness,” the rescue group’s statement said. Officials from the national parks, who led the investigation, said Standish had been attempting to hike the Continental Divide Trail – a hike starting in Canada through to the border of Mexico. This time, he was hiking southbound, after his initial northbound attempt in 2024. Standish had been giving his family back home in Australia regular updates via his Garmin, with an update sent on July 19 planning out his next movements. On July 23, his family received a check-in with no coordinates or message, but a video on Facebook Messenger, which they believed placed him in the Tetons. By July 27, when they hadn’t heard anything else, they contacted park officials.



By Wednesday morning, two days later, the search and rescue helicopter flew a team to Standish’s last presumed point, and, from the air, saw a bright orange backpack. Then, they found him. “His body was recovered and transported to TCSAR headquarters in Jackson before being transferred to the Teton County Coroner’s Office,” the rescue group said. Will (left) with his siblings Jess and George. “TCSAR sends its sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased, and wishes to express its gratitude to the partnering federal agencies who assisted in the investigation.” Sharing her grief, trail friend Katie Jackson also took to social media to farewell the hiker, who she said had a “uniquely large heart”.



“Struck this week by the enormity of the choices we make: where we go, what we do, and especially who we go with,” she wrote. “Incredibly grateful to have known Will so well and experienced how his life touched and changed mine. “Will had a uniquely large heart that was filled to the brim with love from and for his family, friends, adventures, tiny foster puppies, music, snowboarding, and comically large burritos. To know him was to spend most of your day laughing.” Will Standish pictured with his mum Ann. The Continental Divide Trail Coalition said they’d lost someone who lifted everyone up.



“The CDT community lost a bit of light this week,” they said in a Facebook post following his death. “Though he began his 2026 hike stronger than ever, Will was reported overdue on July 26. Concerned hikers immediately rallied to spread the word and join the search, which was a bit of comfort to his worried family in Australia. “At CDTC, like so many others, we are deeply saddened by the news of Will’s passing.” Since his death in the US, Standish’s trail friends started a fundraiser to help pay for his funeral, and the heavy price of bringing him home to Australia. Will Standish (middle) pictured with siblings Jess and George, his dad Dave, and his mum Ann.



A DFAT spokesperson said they were providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian who died in Wyoming. “We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time,” they said in a statement. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: What’s more important, integrity or cabinet solidarity?
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters What’s more important, integrity or cabinet solidarity? August 2, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. VICTORIA Ben Carroll’s first sit-down interview as premier is revealing (″⁣Big Ben strikes″⁣, 2/8). We learn that although he considers ″⁣integrity is non-negotiable″⁣, he, at the same time, maintains that ″⁣when cabinet arrives at a decision you need to support that position″⁣.

We also learn that although he has ″⁣been wanting transparency and accountability for a long time″⁣, we should simply accept his private estimation that ″⁣the SRL [project] does have merit and does need to continue″⁣.

But he cannot have it both ways: either integrity trumps cabinet solidarity or it does not; and the value of the SRL should be made public or remain a government secret.

What is revealed by Chip Le Grand’s interview, then, is that Carroll is just another platitudinous politician.

Peter Drum, Coburg Tell Dan and Jacinta where to go

In November 1917, Leon Trotsky informed his main opponents, the Mensheviks: “Your role is played out. Go where you belong from now on – into the dustbin of history.”

It would appear that Ben Carroll is telling his erstwhile colleagues, Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, to do the same, (″⁣Big Ben strikes″⁣, 2/8).

Ivan Glynn, Vermont



Boring machines, start your engines

Thank you, Premier Carroll for your commitment to build the SRL. While I agree with him that the SRL was initially badly planned, it is nonetheless a great project.

Yes, there are problems, but I note that recent large contracts have come under budget and the project is broadly on time. Also, it comes under considerable ongoing management particularly with the addition of federal government financial oversight.

It is far too late to consider any other course but to get on with it, as the premier said ″⁣that era is over″⁣. I look forward to the tunnel-boring machines starting their march forward in the next few weeks with the future promise of a world-class, integrated train system and service.

Timothy Hoffmann, Brunswick SRL will be obsolete in 2050

″⁣Why didn’t we build the SRL, like every other major world city which has one?″⁣ asks a correspondent (Letters, ″⁣City needs the SRL″⁣, 2/8) imagining a question asked in 2050.

Because, like Los Angeles and other 21st century cities, we will have implemented driverless taxis to minimise congestion, lower emissions, reduce travel time and improve general mobility.

A fleet of autonomous on-demand taxis or mini buses offering almost door-to-door transport will render the SRL a very expensive tunnel for a tiny herd of white elephants.

And dare I say it? Melbourne should maintain a stable and almost sustainable population through regionalisation and fast country rail – just like ″⁣every other major world city″⁣.

James Richardson, Langwarrin Evidence-based decisions need explaining

It is understandable that Ben Carroll aims to distance himself from his immediate predecessors (″⁣Carroll’s long run: Can the boy from Airport West outrun Andrews’ ghost?″⁣ 1/8).

However, I hope he doesn’t throw out policies that are based on evidence, which he believes is so important. The article suggested that Carroll has questioned the current Labor policy of phasing out gas connections in Victoria.

The evidence is clear that burning fossil fuels contributes to dangerous climate change.

If this policy is reversed, the premier would need to clearly explain the evidence on which this action was taken.

Judy Williams, Beaumaris THE FORUM



The long view

Peter Hartcher reminds us of the importance of reducing the national deficit (“One bold, fiscal move would ease our economic anxiety. Does the PM have the nerve?“, 1/8) while Caitlin Fitzsimmons (“Rewarding companies to do nothing is undermining Australia’s climate cuts”, 1/8) makes the argument for a massive cut in fuel rebates for mining and resource companies. So. there is part of the solution to the budget challenge Peter refers to.

And, if we also bring in the proposed 25 per cent tax for gas exports, a move that is widely supported across the community, then the task of reducing the national deficit will become significantly easier.

If we are to have a country that can survive and thrive through the coming years of climate disasters and international uncertainties, we must have governments that take the long view, and are prepared to stand up to some of the corporate interests.

Catherine Rossiter, Fadden, ACT Great visionary

Alfred Deakin came into the world on this day 170 years ago (August 3, 1856), and lived a life worthy of admiration and emulation, eventually serving three times as prime minister.

Elected as a young man to the Victorian parliament, Deakin astonished colleagues in his first speech by resigning – owing to electoral irregularities that weighed on his conscience.

He failed at the ensuing byelection, but eventually regained a seat, enabling him to secure occupational health and safety in factories, compensation for injuries, and limiting exorbitant hours.

But his greatest achievement was helping to found the nation through his writings, exertions and spoken remarks, including this at the 1897 Adelaide Federation Convention: “We are trustees for posterity, for the unborn millions, unknown and unnumbered, whose aspirations we may help to fulfil and whose destinies we may assist to determine.“

David D’Lima, Sturt, SA Modern party politics

The alleged shenanigans of Christian Ellis and the Reformers as revealed by ICAC last week are enough to give political parties a bad name! (“The 11-hour drive and profane putdown: Inside the meeting that killed a Liberal Party takeover”, 2/8).

A covert factional meeting up in ‘Them Thar Hills’, suggestions of money nonchalantly passed under the table and furtive turnings of heads, an eleven-hour car race against time and a heroic female protagonist saving the day, albeit temporarily.

Yes, throw in the potential involvement of Carmelite nuns, unbeknown to them. Not to forget loyal elderly acolytes, past their use-by date, being thrown under the bus.

Slapstick comedy? No party politics at work. No wonder Australians are fed up.

Jennifer Quigley, Balwyn Europe on fire

The wildfires ravaging Europe are a tragedy, and as in Australia and California, are an annual occurrence in the summer. There has been some commentary relating these fires to climate change, however the main causes seem to be more easily explained.

For example, more than 300 people have been arrested in France during this fire season for either arson or not following fire safety regulations. These reasons account for nine out of 10 wildfires.

Climate change may be the cause of some of these fires ,however in the vast majority of cases, it’s attributable to the negligence of humans.

These reckless acts are not specific to France or any other country, they are prevalent in most jurisdictions, just like any other crime.

Christo Krousoratis, Templestowe Blazes offer clue

The unfortunate and unusual wildfires in Europe, to me, are a sure sign that the planet is struggling, but strangely, not a word from our resident climate denier Tony Abbott telling us it’s a hoax.

Greg Bardin, Altona North



DYI medicine

As a retired dental surgeon, I was appalled, but hardly surprised, by the report on Byte dental aligners (″⁣No oversight: Dental aligners leave a trail of woe″⁣, 2/8).

I was just as appalled by the use of do-it-yourself mouthguards, which were readily available during my years of practice – and probably still are – and were much cheaper than getting a mouthguard professionally constructed.

Social media has much to answer for, making dangerous appliances attractive and cheap and too many people go for the cheaper option ignorant of the dangers and risks.

Professional services are certainly not cheap, but with them comes professional qualifications and experience and oversight by professional associations and legal requirements.

Inherent risks are always present to some extent in procedures, but these are explained by practitioners in order to get patients’ informed consent to treatment.

This does not occur with internet or over the counter remedies.

What next? Do it yourself appendectomies.

Can’t be all that difficult and certainly cheaper that paying a surgeon the gap after Medicare.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick Stardust memories

We all know the past is another country. Tony Wright’s “Claret at 11am and Nescaf in the rearview: coming of age in a Carlton wonderland”, 1/8) has conjured up a time long ago.

As a Melbourne University student in the early 1960s, I remember so clearly the joys of remaking the world over coffee in the caf.

University was not just sitting in lectures or the library, trying to catch the eye of that cute boy but a lesson in finding one’s way in that world.

And oh, the joy of deciding yes, lunch at Jimmy Watson’s, throwing the steak on his barbecue and delighting in the glass of wine to go with it. These were indeed the days.

Miriam Gould, Malvern Victim blaming

Whether intended or not, former Tourism Victoria CEO Lois Appleby’s plea to “clean the city up” (Letters, ″⁣Melbourne, wake up″⁣, 30/7) because she had to navigate around homeless people in the CBD, makes it sound like they are the problem, rather than a symptom of the growing inequity in this country.

The only way to improve this situation is for our society to decide we want to reverse this trend, which is leaving more and more people behind.

Tanya Matheson, Ascot Vale Visceral reaction

I shook with fury after reading Andrew Furhmann’s review of Stephanie Lake Company’s Vista – “Energy and chaos can’t mask drab material”, 31/7.

He is consistently disrespectful of many dance works and I believe that readers deserve more informed commentary on this art form.

Susan Bendall, Elwood Overheard

I loved Roby D’Ottavi’s article ″⁣I love eavesdropping but there are things I shouldn’t have to hear in public″⁣ (2/8). I recently lost a dear friend who had made eavesdropping into an art form. She especially loved restaurants where the tables are so close together you can’t help but become involved in the minutae of others’ private lives.

Some years ago we were lunching in a pub in Adelaide and two young women came in, with no pause in their conversation when they sat down near us.

″⁣Well!″⁣ said one, ″⁣I woke up in his flat and he had, like, nothing!″⁣

″⁣Oh my god!″⁣ her friend replied.

″⁣I know! Thank god I’d taken my own hair-straightener!″⁣

Gabrielle Gardner, Montmorency



Sterling stuff

Re Justin Hurwitz, inviting our newest maestro, Sterling Nasa, (the hero that saved the night in Sydney two months ago) – to play piano again – this time at the La La Land concert in Los Angeles (″⁣Audience member Sterling Nasa performs in Justin Hurwitz’s La La Land In Concert″⁣, 2/8).

What a Sterling idea, Mr Hurwitz.

Jason Apostolou, St Kilda How to lose your mind

The anger and frustration Waleed Aly writes about “Forgot Password?” (31/7) is very real. Recently, my husband was admitted to hospital multiple times, and each time pathology tests were performed. Nine separate invoices, delivered via SMS text, ask us to pay the gap fees for these tests.

Concerned about scams, we rang the number provided on the invoice. A message said ″⁣we are experiencing slightly longer waiting times than usual” and “please continue to hold”.

No matter what time of the day I ring, nobody ever answers.

The text on the phone is minute, payment requires toggling between screens and transcribing reference and invoice numbers and my bank details. Potential for errors in the process is huge. This must be done separately for all nine invoices. The help line continues to be experiencing “longer than usual wait times”. An email request for hard copies to be sent is fruitless.

Yesterday, a tenth invoice arrived, again via SMS text, but this time from a debt collection agency. In order to check it is legitimate, I go to the “Need More Information” which asks I provide my personal details, not something I’m prepared to do when I’m trying to check the authenticity of the company.

The total for all bills is less than $150. When the pathology company can provide me with invoices which I can cross-check and pay the outstanding amount in one transaction, not ten, I will happily pay.

Heather Saunders, Warrnambool AND ANOTHER THING Commonwealth Games

Australians all let us rejoice by celebrating the achievements of our athletes at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games with glee.
